work_order.understanding: #37 collects five non-blocking findings from the review of #36. Four are live code defects in the opportunity/experiment surface and are fixed here; the fifth is a PR-hygiene action on an already-merged commit and is answered in out_of_scope. Finding 1 (opportunity money stored in raw currency units, not micros) is the root cause and finding 2 (unguarded expectedContribution) is closed at the same time by the same change, because requiring value/cost to be safe-integer micros removes the overflow entirely. Findings 3 and 4 are independent one-line honesty fixes in the evaluate response and the experiment card. This is a pre-release, local-first app whose money invariant is stated twice (conventions.md and TR-1/TR-20) and whose experiments table already names money in micros (max_spend_micros), so the opportunities record is the outlier and should be brought in line. I (the arbiter) re-derived all four pinned scores and both pinned contributions by hand and confirmed they are preserved exactly by the micros rename (the score is scale-free and the x1e6 in the contribution cancels).
work_order.root_cause: The opportunities record was modelled with value and cost as bare floats in raw major currency units, converted to micros only inside expectedContribution via a hardcoded x1e6. That single float unit is the shared cause of two findings: it violates the micros invariant (TR-1/TR-20, conventions.md, money.js header), and because a validated float can be as large as ~1.8e308, expectedContribution multiplies it by 1e6 with no bound and returns Infinity, which JSON-serialises as null on the wire — the exact overflow the score guards against two functions above but the contribution does not. Fixing the unit (safe-integer micros) removes the conversion, bounds the arithmetic, and renders the two screens consistently. The remaining two findings are independent: the evaluate route discards evaluations.append's return value, and the experiment card emits its caps twice.
work_order.approach:
Four changes, all in the opportunity/experiment surface already covered by #36.

(1) Opportunity money -> integer micros (fixes finding 1, and the value half of finding 2). In src/domain/opportunities.js rename the two money components value->value_micros and cost->cost_micros, matching the max_spend_micros naming already in the experiments record. The score is scale-free because value_micros/cost_micros equals value/cost, so all four pinned scores are preserved exactly (GENERIC 2.16, EXPENSIVE 0.9208, CHEAP 0.40, LOW 0.01). The one subtlety: the cost divisor floor must scale with the unit — it was DIVISOR_FLOOR=1 raw unit, it becomes MICROS_PER_UNIT=1_000_000 (one currency unit in micros) so the zero-cost case still scores 216 (432_000_000/1_000_000/2/1). downside and delay are dimensionless multipliers, not money, so their floors stay at 1. Rewrite scoreOpportunity's floor line to floor cost_micros at MICROS_PER_UNIT and downside/delay at 1 (no longer a uniform DIVISORS.map). In validateOpportunity, value_micros and cost_micros are validated as non-negative safe integers under OPP_BAD_MONEY (instead of 'finite float, non-negative'), while the other six components keep their finite-number check. The existing numerator-product finite guard is kept and stays reachable (a safe-integer value_micros times an unbounded infoValue still overflows).

(2) expectedContribution is total (closes finding 2). With micros stored, the x1e6 line disappears entirely: expectedContribution = trunc(value_micros * pSuccess) - cost_micros. The expensive/cheap contributions are unchanged (1_700_000_000 and 300_000_000). Because a validated value_micros is a safe integer (<= 9.007e15) and pSuccess <= 1, the product can never overflow, so the wire value is never null. As defence-in-depth for direct callers that bypass validation (mirroring scoreOpportunity's existing 'unscorable record returns 0' guard), expectedContribution returns 0 when the result is not a finite safe integer.

(3) Evaluate response surfaces the append result (fixes finding 3). In src/api/routes.js capture the {appended} returned by repositories.evaluations.append (currently discarded) and add appended and duplicate: !appended to the evaluate response, mirroring the raw-events POST precedent ({appended, duplicate: !appended}). The mutable experiments row is still rewritten regardless, but the append-only evaluation record is no longer silently dropped without a word on the wire.

(4) Experiment card renders caps once (fixes finding 4). In src/web/pages.js put data-testid="caps" on the prose span and delete the redundant div immediately below it. The test currently passes against either copy, so a new assertion counts the occurrences inside a single card and pins it to exactly one.

Readability half of finding 1: the opportunity row rendered components through a bare String(), so a reader could not tell 1900 from micros. In the same pages.js change, the two money components (value_micros, cost_micros) render through the existing money() helper as rupee amounts (the helper at pages.js:188-190 renders the U+20B9 sign, so the rendered value is e.g. ₹6000.00); the six dimensionless components stay as plain numbers. IMPORTANT: preserve the existing `?? '—'` fallback for the two money components — render `row.components[key] == null ? '—' : money(row.components[key])` — so a legacy-shaped or missing component shows the '—' placeholder rather than '₹NaN' (money(undefined) would otherwise produce '₹NaN', and a pre-existing local DB row that still carries value/cost has components.value_micros === undefined). The web test asserts ₹6000.00 / ₹1900.00 appear, the bare 6000000000 does not, and a legacy-shaped component renders '—'.

Callers found by grep (all updated): validateOpportunity/scoreOpportunity in src/api/routes.js (POST /v1/opportunities) and scripts/seed.js; expectedContribution in src/api/routes.js only; the components object is built in src/data/repositories.js shape() and consumed by src/web/pages.js opportunityRow and the GET /v1/opportunities response; the record is stored as an opaque JSON column (opportunities.record TEXT), so no SQL migration is needed and the experiments record already names caps in micros.

risks: Renaming value/cost to value_micros/cost_micros is a breaking change to the POST /v1/opportunities request body and to the stored opportunity JSON record. This is acceptable in v1 (local-first, no external consumers, API introduced in #36), but the acceptance must run against a fresh DB.

The cost divisor floor changing from 1 to 1_000_000 is the one non-obvious part of the unit change; getting it wrong silently rescales the zero-cost score away from the pinned 216. The zero-cost test guards it.
expectedContribution returning 0 for a direct overflowing call is a display-field sentinel, matching scoreOpportunity's existing unscorable-returns-0 convention; it is never a sort key.
out_of_scope: Finding 5 (drive-by change to test/api/decisions.test.js): the fix is already present in main — maturedBody derives decided_at and evaluation.evaluated_at from one sampled instant, exactly as the reviewer recommended, and the flake it fixes is real. The reviewer's only action was to split commit 55ffb5c out of #36's diff as a separate PR for review hygiene. #36 is already merged into main (04730fc), and the fix arrived in that squash, so there is no commit left to split and rewriting merged history to split it is not appropriate. The correct fix is retained; no code change is made for this finding.

Adding a SQL migration for the opportunities table: the money lives inside the opaque opportunities.record JSON column, not in typed columns, so the unit change is purely in the domain/record shape and needs no ALTER TABLE.
Converting the opportunities seed to a backfill for pre-existing databases: this is a pre-release local-first app; operators re-seed on a fresh DB (see risks).
work_order.confidence_rationale: I re-derived every load-bearing number by hand rather than trusting the proposal: the four scores (2.16, 0.9208, 0.40, 0.01) are preserved because value_micros/cost_micros equals value/cost; the zero-cost score stays 216 because the cost floor scales to 1_000_000 micros (432_000_000/1_000_000/2/1 = 216); both contributions (1_700_000_000, 300_000_000) are preserved because the x1e6 cancels. I read the full domain file and confirmed the proposal's description of it is exact (raw floats, the x1e6 fudge, the uniform DIVISOR_FLOOR=1 map, the unguarded contribution). Finding 2 was reproduced live (expectedContribution -> Infinity -> JSON null). Findings 1, 3, 4 were confirmed by reading the exact code and the full caller set was grepped. I verified all three of the critique's findings against the source myself and found each one founded, so the plan going into implementation has no known unhandled execution break. The number is not 90+ because two non-load-bearing unknowns remain: the breaking record-shape change requires a fresh DB (mitigated by the kept '—' guard so stale rows degrade gracefully rather than showing ₹NaN), and the rename of the request/record keys is a judgement call I have made in the issue body's favour but that a human could reasonably reverse — the score and contribution values are identical either way, so nothing load-bearing rests on it.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep opportunity value/cost in raw currency units and only document that choice in the module header, formatting the opportunity row with money().
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: This is the reviewer's fallback, but it leaves opportunities holding money in a unit no other table uses, in direct conflict with conventions.md ("Money, timestamps and identifiers follow the invariants: micros"), TR-1/TR-20, and money.js's explicit "Floats never enter storage, APIs and this module". It also leaves expectedContribution's x1e6 conversion and its overflow exposure in place, so findings 1 and 2 both stay half-open. Since the score is provably scale-free, the clean fix costs nothing in correctness.

alternatives_considered.approach: Add a validation guard to expectedContribution returning 0 on overflow, without changing the stored unit (treat finding 2 as a standalone one-line fix).
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Hides the symptom without fixing the root cause: raw-unit float storage still violates the micros invariant (finding 1) and still allows values above ~1.8e302 that the guard would mask as 0 rather than reject. Fixing the unit closes both findings at the source with fewer moving parts than a guard plus a rename.

alternatives_considered.approach: Reject the overflowing input in validateOpportunity (extend the existing numerator-product guard to the contribution) rather than making expectedContribution total.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: A safe-integer value_micros times pSuccess <= 1 can no longer overflow, so there is nothing left to reject once the unit is fixed, and a guard on a computation that cannot overflow is dead code. The return-0 fallback is kept only for direct callers that bypass validation, mirroring scoreOpportunity's existing unscorable-returns-0 convention.

alternatives_considered.approach: Split the four code findings into separate work orders / PRs.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Findings 1 and 2 share a single root cause and a single change in src/domain/opportunities.js; splitting them would either duplicate the unit change or split a coherent fix. Findings 3 and 4 touch the same files (routes.js, pages.js) as the read surface of finding 1, and each is one line. One work order is the smaller honest change.

assumptions: Renaming the request-body and record fields value/cost to value_micros/cost_micros is acceptable for a v1 local-first API with no external consumers (introduced in #36); the issue body's own fix recommendation names value_micros/cost_micros to match max_spend_micros.

downside and delay are dimensionless multipliers, not money, so only value and cost become micros. This is inferred from the fixtures (downside 2, delay 1) and from the spec formula, which lists them as separate score components alongside money.
The opportunities.record column is opaque JSON, so no SQL migration and no column-level money typing is required; the unit change is confined to the domain and the record shape.

The existing numerator-product finite guard remains correct and necessary after the unit change, because infoValue is an unbounded multiplier and a safe-integer value_micros times a huge infoValue can still overflow.

A pre-existing local app.db will hold stale-shaped opportunity records after this change, and re-seeding on a fresh DB is the supported path; the kept '—' guard means a stale row degrades to a placeholder rather than '₹NaN'.
unknowns: Whether any external consumer (none in this repo) reads the opportunity value/cost keys; only src/api/routes.js, src/data/repositories.js, src/web/pages.js and scripts/seed.js were found by grep.
The exact reproduction frequency of the finding-3 same-millisecond collision was not measured; the defect (discarded return value) is confirmed by code reading regardless.
work_order.debate_summary: The critique was right on all three of its findings and I folded every one in; I found nothing to dismiss. I re-checked each against the source myself rather than accepting it. Finding 1 (Rs vs the U+20B9 sign): confirmed — money() at pages.js:188-190 renders ₹, grep finds no 'Rs' anywhere in src/ or test/, and the proposal's AC-6, web test and qa_script all said 'Rs', so taken literally those verification steps would have failed against the code the plan told the implementer to write. I corrected the plan's text to the rupee sign throughout rather than touching money(), which is correct. Finding 2 (the re-post assertion): confirmed — test/api/opportunities.test.js:300 asserts repost.components.value === 6000, which the value->value_micros rename breaks, and the proposal's test list never mentioned the re-post test; I added an explicit case to update it to value_micros === 6_000_000_000. Finding 3 (the lost '—' guard): confirmed and the subtlest of the three — the current opportunityRow deliberately renders `row.components[key] ?? '—'`, and routing the two money components through money() would replace that placeholder with '₹NaN' (money(undefined) === '₹NaN', verified) for exactly the legacy-shaped rows the plan's own assumption says will exist on a pre-existing local DB. I specified the guard explicitly in the pages.js change and added a test. Where I disagree with the plan is only on one framing: the proposal recorded as an unknown whether the rename should happen at all; the issue body itself recommends value_micros/cost_micros to match max_spend_micros, so I settled it in the rename's favour and dropped that unknown. The proposal's diagnosis, root cause, and four-part approach I re-derived independently and they hold — the four pinned scores, the zero-cost 216 (which depends on the subtle cost-floor rescale to 1_000_000 micros, and which I recomputed as 432_000_000/1_000_000/2/1), and both pinned contributions are all preserved. The three findings are execution and verification errors, not a wrong diagnosis, exactly as the critique itself said, so the plan's spine is unchanged and only its text and its test list grew. net: the critique made this work order correct on three real points without changing what the work is.
residual_risks: The request-body and stored-record key rename is a breaking change for any pre-existing local app.db; QA must run against a fresh, freshly-seeded DB (the qa_script does this).

The one genuinely load-bearing subtlety is the cost divisor floor rescaling to MICROS_PER_UNIT (1_000_000) in scoreOpportunity; if it is missed, the zero-cost score silently leaves 216 and the EXPENSIVE/CHEAP/LOW scores shift. The zero-cost and four-pinned-score tests in test/domain/opportunities.test.js are the guard — QA should check those first.

The evaluate appended/duplicate addition was checked by the critique and is sound on every path (evaluateExperiment always returns a truthy outcome on the non-error path, so the append always runs before the 200 and the two new fields are always present); there is no falsy-outcome case to handle.
